newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine reshuffle not over yet, says Kuchma aide.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine reshuffle not over yet, says Kuchma aide.

text.p: A cabinet reshuffle by President Leonid Kuchma did little to dispel economic uncertainty in Ukraine on Wednesday and a senior presidential aide said the clear-out was not over yet.

Analysts said Tuesday's sackings of four ministers reflected political rivalries and were unlikely to help the economy. Some said the action might unsettle the atmosphere at a time when Kiev is seeking a new IMF loan.

But the secretary of the policy-making security and defence council said more dismissals could follow. "These are essential changes and these changes will continue," Volodymyr Horbulin, Kuchma's closest aide, told a news briefing.
Horbulin made clear that Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, whose criticism of the ministers at a cabinet session last Friday preceded the dismissals, was safe -- at least for now.
"Two or three days ago the Ukrainian prime minister said his own position was fairly stable. I agree with him," he said.

Analysts interpreted the sackings of finance minister Valentyn Koronevsky, statistics minister Olexander Osaulenko, economy minister Vasyl Hureyev and the minister for machine-building and the military complex as a pre-emptive strike to save Lazarenko.
A raft of economic troubles has sparked criticism from across the political spectrum and brought miners, teachers and other workers onto the streets in protest in recent months.

A non-payments crisis has left workers unpaid for months, gross domestic product fell 10.4 percent last month compared to January of last year and the government has failed so far to win parliament's approval for this year's budget and tax reforms.
But economists said the real problems lay in the economy itself and sacking ministers would not help, particularly when new policies were being put in place.
"This is unnerving and unsettling. It can't be a good thing, in that there's no stability and continuity," one analyst said.
"I can't imagine the IMF (International Monetary Fund) will believe that their replacements will be the salvation of the Ukrainian economy," the analyst added.
Ukraine hopes to win a $2.5-$3 billion Extended Fund Facility loan from the IMF this year to take over from a $860 million stand-by loan.
Ukrainian currency dealers said the sacking of Koronevsky would have no impact on the Treasury-bill and currency markets as he did not define policies in those areas.
Kuchma, Lazarenko and central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko are seen as controlling financial and economic policies in the former Soviet republic of 52 million.

One Western diplomat said that none of the sacked ministers were "particulary creative" while another said Koronevsky had said so little about financial policy that he had become known as "the silent one".

Horbulin hinted that Ihor Mityukov, a former deputy finance minister, could take over from Koronevsky, a theory backed up by government sources and several deputies in parliament who said he was the best available option.
He confirmed that Mityukov, Yuri Yekhanurov, chairman of the state property fund and Hureyev would soon meet Kuchma, who was on holiday in western Ukraine.

"These three ministers...will meet the president. A proposal will be made to them but it would be tactless of me to answer before they have met. A situation could arise where the president fails to reach an agreement with them," Horbulin said.
Therew was some speculation that Hureyev would move to machine-building and Yekhanurov would take over at the economy ministry.
"I cannot rule out that the appointments will be decided by the president today or tomorrow," Horbulin said.
